_comment: Everybody Left From Here. Twelve stops from Borough High Street to Rotherhithe, about four kilometres and two hours, written round people and the things that happened to them rather than round buildings. The brief asked for about an hour and then for Borough to Rotherhithe, which cannot both be had: the intro says so and marks Tower Bridge, stop six, as the hour mark. Everything is outdoors and free. Seven questions, five location gates, and the last stop is a pub. Every coordinate, plaque, sculpture and pub named here came out of data/osm/borough-rotherhithe.json. The five archived London themes were City themes and none of their thirty stops is south of the river, so this is new writing; the one thing carried over is the old London Bridge material from the St Magnus stop, which belongs at the Southwark end anyway.
name: Everybody Left From Here
tagline: pilgrims, prisoners and emigrants, along four kilometres of south bank

intro.lead: Twelve stops from Borough to Rotherhithe.
intro.body:
Four kilometres along the south bank, about two hours with the stops. It is flat.

Six ask a question you can only answer by looking. Six just need you standing in the right place.

Everything is outdoors and free. If you only have an hour, break off at Tower Bridge, which is number six.
intro.start: Start in Angel Place, the narrow alley beside the library off Borough High Street.

topics.name: Pilgrims and Prisoners
topics.blurb: Everyone going south left from this street, and some of them were not allowed to leave at all.

topics.name: The Working River
topics.blurb: Four hundred years of bridges, wharves and slums, on one bend of the Thames.

topics.name: The Ships That Left
topics.blurb: A tunnel under the water, a church full of sailors, and the stairs one ship sailed from.

outro:
Twelve stops, and you are at the pub.

The engine house and the church are both a few minutes back up the road. Rotherhithe station is five minutes the same way.

If you have more walking in you, the path carries on east past the old dock entrances towards Greenwich.

stops.title: The Wall in Angel Place
stops.where: Angel Place, the narrow alley beside the library

question.ask: A famous writer's father was locked up here. Who was the writer?
question.hint: The plaque names him. He was twelve at the time.

stops.look:
A brick wall down one side of a narrow alley. It is the last piece of the Marshalsea, a prison for people who owed money.

You could not leave until you paid, and there was no way to earn it inside.
stops.after:
Charles Dickens. His father John was brought here in February 1824 owing a baker forty pounds.

Charles was twelve. He was taken out of school and sent to paste labels on pots in a blacking factory by the river, six days a week.

He put the prison in Little Dorrit. He never told his own children any of it.
stops.after_spoken:
Charles Dickens. His father John was brought here in February eighteen twenty four owing a baker forty pounds.

Charles was twelve. He was taken out of school and sent to paste labels on pots in a blacking factory by the river, six days a week.

He put the prison in Little Dorrit. He never told his own children any of it.

stops.title: Talbot Yard
stops.where: the plaque in Talbot Yard, off Borough High Street
stops.directions:
Follow Angel Place west out to Borough High Street, then turn right and go north up it. About four hundred metres.

Talbot Yard is a narrow opening on the right. The plaque is on the wall inside.

question.ask: Pilgrims set off from an inn here in a famous book. Who wrote it?
question.hint: His name is on the plaque, with the name of the inn.

stops.look:
The Tabard stood in this yard. It was one of many inns along this road.

They are all gone now, but the yards still carry their names.
stops.after:
Geoffrey Chaucer. The Canterbury Tales begins at the Tabard, where twenty-nine pilgrims meet and agree to tell stories on the road.

He wrote it in the thirteen eighties. The inn was real and so was the landlord, Harry Bailly, who turns up in the book under his own name.

It burned in 1676, was rebuilt, and was pulled down in 1873.
stops.after_spoken:
Geoffrey Chaucer. The Canterbury Tales begins at the Tabard, where twenty-nine pilgrims meet and agree to tell stories on the road.

He wrote it in the thirteen eighties. The inn was real and so was the landlord, Harry Bailly, who turns up in the book under his own name.

It burned in sixteen seventy six, was rebuilt, and was pulled down in eighteen seventy three.

stops.title: The George
stops.where: the yard in front of the George Inn
stops.directions:
Out of Talbot Yard, turn right and go north up Borough High Street, then take the next opening on the right. About ninety metres.

The George is at the end of the yard, on the left.

gate.prompt: Stand in the yard, in front of the galleries.

stops.look:
Two tiers of open wooden gallery along the front. Coaches pulled into this yard and passengers walked round the balconies to their rooms.

London once had dozens of galleried coaching inns. This is the only one left.
stops.after:
The National Trust owns it now.

The building went up after the Southwark fire of 1676. Two of its three sides were pulled down in the eighteen eighties to make room for a railway yard.

Dickens drank here.
stops.after_spoken:
The National Trust owns it, which saved it.

What stands here went up after the Southwark fire of sixteen seventy six. Two of its three sides came down in the eighteen eighties, to clear space for a railway yard. You are looking at a third of it.

Dickens drank here.

stops.title: Southwark Cathedral
stops.where: the churchyard on the north side of the cathedral
stops.directions: From the George, head north through the market. About three hundred metres. The lanes are narrow and busy on a market day.

gate.prompt: Stand in the churchyard, on the north side.

stops.look:
Two men were here in the same year, 1607.

One was buried in this church that December, the other baptised in it that November.

There is a university named after one of them.
stops.look_spoken:
Two men were here in the same year, sixteen oh seven.

One was buried in this church that December. The other was baptised in it that November.

There is a university named after the second one.
stops.after:
Edmund Shakespeare, William's youngest brother and an actor like him. He died at twenty-seven, and William paid twenty shillings for a forenoon knell of the great bell, the expensive option.

John Harvard was a butcher's son from this parish. He went to Massachusetts, died at thirty, and left his books and half his money to a new college outside Boston.
stops.directions_target: the cathedral, and the churchyard on its north side

stops.title: Old London Bridge
stops.where: the mosaic on the riverside walk, near Hay's Galleria
stops.directions: From the cathedral, head east to the river, then downstream. About five hundred and fifty metres.

question.ask: The mosaic shows the old bridge. What was built along the whole length of it?
question.hint: Look at the skyline in the picture. It is not a bare crossing.

stops.look:
A picture in tile, showing London Bridge at night in the fifteenth century.

For more than five hundred years it was the only bridge over the Thames in London.
stops.after:
Houses and shops, seven storeys high in places, leaning out over the water.

There was a chapel on it, and a gatehouse at the Southwark end where the heads of traitors were set on poles. A German visitor counted thirty of them in 1598.

The buildings came off in 1762 and the bridge was replaced in 1831.
stops.after_spoken:
Houses and shops, seven storeys high in places, leaning out over the water.

There was a chapel on it, and a gatehouse at the Southwark end where the heads of traitors were set on poles. A German visitor counted thirty of them in fifteen ninety eight.

The buildings came off in seventeen sixty two and the bridge itself went in eighteen thirty one.
stops.directions_target: a mosaic of an old bridge, set into the wall on the landward side

stops.title: Tower Bridge
stops.where: the southern end of Tower Bridge
stops.directions: From the mosaic, keep the water on your left and carry on south east. About six hundred metres, all of it on the riverside walk.

gate.prompt: Stand at the southern end of the bridge.

stops.look:
Both halves still lift, about eight hundred times a year.

The stonework is a shell. Underneath it the whole thing is a steel frame, dressed in stone to match the Tower across the water.
stops.after:
It opened in 1894, after eight years of building.

On 30 December 1952 a number 78 bus was crossing when the two halves began to rise under it. The driver, Albert Gunter, put his foot down and jumped the gap.

Nobody was badly hurt. He was given ten pounds.
stops.after_spoken:
It opened in eighteen ninety four, after eight years of building.

On the thirtieth of December nineteen fifty two a number seventy eight bus was crossing when the two halves began to rise under it. The driver, Albert Gunter, put his foot down and jumped the gap.

Nobody was badly hurt. He was given ten pounds.
stops.directions_target: the southern end of Tower Bridge

stops.title: St Saviour's Dock
stops.where: the footbridge across the mouth of the dock
stops.directions: From the bridge, head south east between the warehouses. About five hundred metres, down a narrow street with high brick on both sides.

gate.prompt: Stand on the footbridge over the creek.

stops.look:
A tidal creek between warehouses. A small river called the Neckinger comes out here.

The slum on the far side was called Jacob's Island: a maze of ditches, plank bridges and rotting timber, with the worst cholera in London.
stops.after:
Dickens killed Bill Sikes here at the end of Oliver Twist, in a chase over the roofs.

He described it so exactly that an alderman stood up in public and announced that no such place existed. Dickens went back and described it again, in more detail.

It was pulled down in the eighteen fifties.
stops.directions_target: a footbridge over a tidal creek, at the end of the warehouses

stops.title: The River Wall
stops.where: Bermondsey Wall East, by the Old Justice
stops.directions: From the footbridge, head south east and then east, keeping near the river. About six hundred and fifty metres.

gate.prompt: Stand on the river side of the road, by the pub.

stops.look:
You are on a river wall. Everything behind you is below the high tide line and always has been.

Look downstream, past the bend. The docks that filled that ground were the biggest timber yards in the country.
stops.after:
On the afternoon of 7 September 1940 the bombers came up the river and the timber caught.

A fire officer out on the water that night said the whole bloody world was on fire. Crews coming back after dark could steer by the glow.

They came back every night for fifty-seven nights running.
stops.after_spoken:
On the afternoon of the seventh of September nineteen forty the bombers came up the river and the timber caught.

A fire officer out on the water that night said the whole bloody world was on fire. The glow was navigation enough for the crews who came back after dark.

They came back every night for fifty-seven nights running.
stops.directions_target: a pub called the Old Justice, on the river side of Bermondsey Wall East

stops.title: King's Stairs Gardens
stops.where: the river side of Bermondsey Wall East, by the gardens
stops.directions:
From the Old Justice, follow Bermondsey Wall East, which runs east along the river wall. About four hundred metres.

The gardens open out on the water side, just before Cathay Street.

question.ask: The girl by the wall. Who was she?
question.hint: A board beside the figures names all three.

stops.look:
Two bronze figures sit in the grass on the river side, and a cat.

The seated one is Alfred Salter. He gave up a Harley Street career to doctor the poorest parish in London, and the parish sent him to Parliament.
stops.after:
Joyce, his daughter. She caught scarlet fever from his patients and died in 1910, aged eight.

The Salters had chosen to live in Bermondsey instead of somewhere safer. They stayed on after she died.

The stone ruin behind you is much older. Edward III built a manor house on this bank in 1353, when it was an island in the marsh.
stops.after_spoken:
Joyce, his daughter. She caught scarlet fever from his patients and died in nineteen ten, aged eight.

The Salters had decided to live in Bermondsey rather than send her somewhere safer. That decision killed her, and they stayed anyway.

The stone ruin behind you is much older. Edward the third built a manor house on this bank in thirteen fifty three, when it was an island in the marsh.

stops.title: The Church at Rotherhithe
stops.where: the churchyard on St Marychurch Street
stops.directions: From the gardens, head east, keeping near the water. About four hundred metres. The path leaves the river for a stretch and comes back.
stops.look:
A red brick church of 1715, paid for by the people who worked the river here.

The master of the ship that carried the Pilgrims to America in 1620 is buried in this churchyard. Nobody wrote down where.
stops.look_spoken:
A red brick church of seventeen fifteen, paid for by the people who worked the river here.

The master of the ship that carried the Pilgrims to America in sixteen twenty is buried in this churchyard. No stone. Nobody wrote down where.
stops.after:
Two timbers of the communion table came out of a warship. The Temeraire was broken up just downstream in 1838. Turner painted her being towed to the yard.

There is also a monument to Prince Lee Boo of Palau. He came to England in 1784, learned English in six months, and died of smallpox inside the year.
stops.after_spoken:
Two timbers of the communion table came out of a warship. The Temeraire was broken up just downstream in eighteen thirty eight. Turner painted her being towed to the yard.

There is also a monument to Prince Lee Boo of Palau. He came to England in seventeen eighty four, learned English in six months, and died of smallpox inside the year.
stops.directions_target: a red brick church on the corner of St Marychurch Street

stops.title: The Engine House
stops.where: the old engine house beside Rotherhithe station
stops.directions:
From the churchyard, go east along Rotherhithe Street, past the station entrance, then right into Tunnel Road. About a hundred and thirty metres.

Look for a squat brick building with a tall chimney.

question.ask: A father and son drove this shaft down and dug east. What was their name?
question.hint: It is on this building, and on the pub up the road.

stops.look:
Low brick, with a chimney. It held the pumps that kept the water out.

The shaft beside it goes down to the first tunnel ever dug under a river that ships used.
stops.after:
The Brunels. Marc designed it and his son Isambard ran the works.

It took eighteen years and the river broke in five times. In 1828 Isambard was washed up the shaft on a wave. Six men behind him drowned. He was twenty-two.

It opened in 1843 as a foot tunnel, and trains use it now.
stops.after_spoken:
The Brunels. Marc designed it and his son Isambard ran the works.

It took eighteen years and the river broke in five times. In eighteen twenty eight Isambard was washed up the shaft on a wave. Six men behind him drowned. He was twenty-two.

It opened in eighteen forty three as a foot tunnel, and trains use it now.

stops.title: The Pub at the Stairs
stops.where: the pub on the river, at the end of St Marychurch Street
stops.directions:
From the engine house, back up Tunnel Road and turn left along Rotherhithe Street, heading west. About sixty metres.

It stands on the river side of the road, and it is the last stop.

nudge.prompt: This is the stop for a drink. The jetty out the back is the place to have it.

question.ask: This pub is named after a ship. Which one?
question.hint: It is on the sign over the door.

stops.look:
Go through to the back if there is room. The pub is built over the old landing stairs.

A ship tied up here in July 1620, took on passengers, and dropped down the coast to pick up the rest.
stops.look_spoken:
Go through to the back if there is room. The pub stands on its own stairs.

A ship tied up here in July sixteen twenty, took on passengers, and dropped down the coast to pick up the rest.
stops.after:
The Mayflower. Her master was Christopher Jones, who lived on this street and lies in the churchyard you have just come from.

She came back the next year and was probably broken up here for timber.

A hundred and two people sailed. About half of them were dead within a year of landing.
